subject: Business Models
title: Platform Leakage
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Platform Leakage.

hook.text: Craigslist lost its jobs section to Indeed, housing to Zillow, and dating to Tinder. Death by 1,000 cuts.

buildup.text: Platform leakage is when specialized competitors peel off individual verticals from a general platform.

discovery.text: Each vertical competitor offers a better experience: better search, curation, and community for that niche.

twist.text: Craigslist still exists and is still profitable. Its simplicity is both its weakness and its survival tool.

climax.text: Horizontal platforms are vulnerable to vertical specialists. Breadth invites unbundling.

punchline.text: Do everything okay, or one thing great. Specialists always attack.

details.summary: Platform leakage occurs when users who met through a platform conduct subsequent transactions outside it to avoid fees. A freelancer found on Upwork communicating directly with clients, or an Airbnb guest booking directly with a host, both represent revenue leakage.
details.whyItMatters: Leakage threatens platform revenue by removing the intermediary after the initial match. Platforms must provide ongoing value beyond matchmaking or implement mechanisms that make staying on the platform more attractive than leaving.
takeaways: Users bypass the platform after initial matching to avoid transaction fees
Leakage is highest when platforms charge high take rates on recurring transactions
Ongoing value like payment protection and dispute resolution reduces leakage

faq.question: How do platforms prevent users from transacting off-platform?
faq.answer: Payment processing with buyer protection, dispute resolution services, reputation systems that only work on-platform, insurance coverage, regulatory compliance tools, and communication monitoring that flags off-platform contact attempts all reduce leakage incentives.

faq.question: When is platform leakage most likely to occur?
faq.answer: When take rates are high, when transactions are recurring between the same parties, when the platform adds little value beyond initial matching, and when trust has already been established between the transacting parties through successful previous interactions.
